headline: GDP growth expected around 0.2% for Q2, with a per capita recession possible given prior quarter contraction — below RBA's ~0.5% expectation
reasoning: Net trade is expected to contribute 0.1 percentage points to GDP, while government spending was positive but soft. The overall picture points to GDP growth of around 0.2%, well below the RBA's expectation of around 0.5%. On a per capita basis, a contraction is possible; combined with last quarter's per capita GDP contraction, Australia could technically be in a per capita recession. This is described as a 'technical blip' but not a positive signal.
quote: When we add everything all together, the picture's looking, uh, pretty weak. Um, I think we'll get GDP growth of around 0.2%. Maybe a bit more. But, um, it's definitely going to be on that low positive side. Um, we're not expecting a contraction in GDP, but once we take that into per capita terms, it wouldn't be surprising at all to see a contraction. And given that we saw a contraction in per capita GDP last quarter, that would mean that, uh, if we do get a contraction in per capita GDP this quarter, we'd be experiencing a per capita recession.
episode_title: Australia’s trade deficit gets a fuel injection

headline: Current account deficit widened to $27.2bn in June quarter, driven by surging oil import costs and record EV imports, partially offset by higher coal and LNG export prices
reasoning: Australia's current account deficit blew out primarily because oil prices surged, making import bills much larger. Record electric vehicle imports also added to the deficit. While the Middle East conflict boosted export prices for coal and LNG, that uplift was insufficient to offset the oil import surge. Australians also switched away from long-haul European travel to cheaper regional destinations, reducing outbound tourist spending by around 12%, though this did little to offset the overall trade imbalance.
quote: Australia's imports are more expensive, as is sort of the main headline. Um, mostly oil prices are way up. And so the amount that we are spending on, uh, imports of oil, it's, it's way up. Uh, that means Australia's imports ballooned and that means the deficit got larger. The the conflict in the Middle East did also boost the price of a lot of Australia's exports, including coal and LNG. But that impact was nowhere near big enough to offset the big rise in, uh, in oil imports.

headline: Outbound Australian tourist spending fell ~12% year-on-year — first dip since Covid — as high oil prices and Middle East conflict reduced long-haul flight availability to Europe
reasoning: The data showed a striking drop in Australian tourist spending abroad, down about 12% from the prior year, marking the first decline since Covid. The actual number of travellers was roughly unchanged, but Australians shifted from expensive long-haul European trips to cheaper, shorter regional destinations like Vietnam, Indonesia, and New Zealand. Fewer Middle East stopovers were available due to the conflict, reducing European route capacity. The net effect was a significant decline in total outbound spending, while the offsetting fall in inbound European visitors was not large enough to compensate.
quote: The number of Australians or the, amount of, uh, tourist money that was spent overseas by Australians was way down about 12% down from from last year. Um, and the first time that we've seen a dip in tourist numbers, uh, since since Covid... because fewer Australians were looking to go to Europe and the USA, get into that warm summer climate. And that's because of the high cost of travel. Um, as well as the lower, lower availability of routes.

headline: RBA likely to hold in September and wait until November, as weak GDP is investment-led rather than consumer-led and the hot inflation outlook remains the dominant concern
reasoning: Despite the soft GDP print coming in below RBA forecasts, the weakness is concentrated in investment rather than household consumption, which has held up reasonably well. Since the RBA is primarily focused on the consumer and inflation dynamics, the weak headline GDP is unlikely to shift their thinking significantly. Oxford Economics expects the September meeting to remain live but believes the RBA will more likely wait until November before acting. Stubborn inflation continues to be the overriding concern.
quote: The softness that we've seen this quarter has been mostly on the investment side. Uh, the household side has actually held up pretty, pretty well. Um, and that's really where the RBA's going to be paying more attention. So probably, uh, the weak GDP growth that we'll see tomorrow won't, won't worry the RBA too much. We still think they're going to be more nervous about the, uh, hot inflation outlook. Um, and so there's the September meeting is is definitely live. We think on balance, they'll probably be more likely to wait until November.
